title: Singleton and Factory Method
scopeHtml: Scope: thread-safe Singleton variants, why Singleton is often an anti-pattern, and Factory Method with before-and-after code.

notes.title: What a creational pattern is
notes.html:
A creational pattern controls how objects get made, so the rest of the code does not hardcode new ConcreteClass() everywhere. Singleton limits how many exist; Factory Method decides which subclass to make; Abstract Factory makes families; Builder assembles complex ones; Prototype copies; Object Pool reuses.

Why care: new glues the caller to one concrete class. Change the class and every caller changes. Creational patterns move that decision into one place.

Worked example. An app has 40 call sites doing new SmsSender(). Product asks to add WhatsApp. Without a creator: edit 40 files, 40 chances for a bug. With one factory: edit 1 file.

Industry examples. Android LayoutInflater, Executors.newFixedThreadPool, Calendar.getInstance(), Spring's BeanFactory, Dagger/Hilt modules.

Everyday analogy. You do not walk into the kitchen and cook; you tell the waiter "pasta" and the kitchen decides how.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the 23 GoF names. Interviewers want to see you pick one for a reason.
  • Using a pattern when a plain constructor is enough.

notes.title: Singleton: the idea
notes.html:
Singleton guarantees exactly one instance of a class and gives a global access point to it. Typical uses: configuration, a logger, a connection pool manager, a metrics registry.

The mechanism: private constructor (nobody else can new it) plus a static method that returns the one instance.

+---------------------------+
| Config                    |
+---------------------------+
| - static instance: Config |
| - values: Map             |
+---------------------------+
| - Config()                |
| + static getInstance()    |
| + get(key): String        |
+---------------------------+

Worked example. Config file is 200 KB and parsed in 15 ms. 1,000 requests/s each parsing it = 15 s of CPU per second, impossible. Parse once, share one instance.

Industry examples. Runtime.getRuntime() in the JDK, Android Application object, Kotlin object, Spring beans (singleton scope, but managed by the container, not by a static field).

Everyday analogy. A country has one president at a time; everyone refers to the same office.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Singleton = global variable". It is global state with a controlled creation, which is exactly why it is risky.
  • Forgetting the private constructor.

notes.title: Singleton variant 1: eager
notes.html:
Create the instance when the class loads. The JVM guarantees class initialization happens once and is thread-safe, so no locks are needed.

public final class Config {
    private static final Config INSTANCE = new Config(); // built at class load
    private Config() { /* load file */ }
    public static Config getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}

Kotlin: object Config { init { /* load */ } } does the same thing; the compiler generates the static field and a class-init block.

Decision gravity. Chosen because it is the simplest correct version. Alternative: lazy. It breaks when construction is expensive and the object may never be used (slow startup, wasted memory) or when construction can throw (the class fails to load with ExceptionInInitializerError). Fully reversible while callers use getInstance().

Common interview traps.

  • Calling eager "not thread-safe". It is safe; the cost is startup time.
  • Heavy work inside a static initializer: one failure poisons the class for the whole process.

notes.title: Singleton variant 2: broken lazy, then synchronized
notes.html:
Lazy means create on first use. The naive version is broken under threads.

public static Config getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {          // thread A and B both see null
        instance = new Config();     // two objects created
    }
    return instance;
}

Fix 1: synchronized on the method. Correct, but every call takes the lock, even after the instance exists.

public static synchronized Config getInstance() { ... }

Worked example. 16 threads call getInstance() 1M times each. An uncontended lock costs about 20 ns, a contended one can be 1,000+ ns. 16M calls x contention can add seconds. The lock is only needed on the first call.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "if (instance == null)" is safe because the window is tiny. It is a real race; it shows up in production under load.
  • Not mentioning the performance cost of method-level synchronized.

notes.title: Singleton variant 3: double-checked locking
notes.html:
Check without a lock, then lock and check again. Fast path has no lock; only the first callers synchronize.

public final class Config {
    private static volatile Config instance; // volatile is mandatory
    private Config() {}
    public static Config getInstance() {
        Config local = instance;
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (Config.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) {
                    instance = local = new Config();
                }
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}

Why volatile. new Config() is three steps: allocate, run constructor, assign the reference. Without volatile, the JIT/CPU may reorder so the reference is published before the constructor finished; another thread sees a non-null but half-built object. Since Java 5 (JSR-133) volatile forbids that reordering.

Kotlin: companion object { @Volatile private var inst: Config? = null; fun get() = inst ?: synchronized(this) { inst ?: Config().also { inst = it } } }.

Decision gravity. Use it only when you need lazy and cannot use the holder idiom. It is easy to get wrong, so it is a reviewer-risk, not a one-way door.

Common interview traps.

  • Omitting volatile (the classic interview bug).
  • Explaining it without being able to say what reordering means.

notes.title: Singleton variant 4: holder idiom and enum
notes.html:
Initialization-on-demand holder is lazy and lock-free, because the JVM initializes a nested class only when first touched, and does so thread-safely.

public final class Config {
    private Config() {}
    private static class Holder { static final Config I = new Config(); }
    public static Config getInstance() { return Holder.I; }
}

Enum singleton (Effective Java, Item 3) is the strongest: the JVM guarantees one instance, and it survives serialization and reflection attacks.

public enum Config { INSTANCE; public String get(String k) { return "..."; } }

Plain singletons can be broken by: reflection (setAccessible(true) on the constructor), serialization (deserializing creates a new object unless you add readResolve()), and multiple class loaders (one "singleton" per loader).

Recommendation to say aloud. Default to the holder idiom, or enum when serialization matters; in Kotlin use object.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing why the holder is lazy (nested class init is deferred).
  • Ignoring reflection and serialization when asked "can this be broken?".

notes.title: Why Singleton is often an anti-pattern
notes.html:
A Singleton is hidden global state, and that hurts testing, clarity and concurrency.

  1. Hidden dependencies. OrderService calls Config.getInstance() inside a method; its constructor does not say it needs Config. You must read the body to know.
  2. Hard to test. Tests share the one instance, so state leaks from test A to test B; you cannot swap in a fake.
  3. Tight coupling. Callers are bound to the concrete class, not an interface.
  4. Concurrency. Mutable shared state needs locks everywhere.
  5. Violates single responsibility. The class does its job and controls its own lifetime.

Before and after:

// BEFORE: hidden, untestable
class PaymentService {
    void pay(Order o) {
        String key = Config.getInstance().get("stripe.key");   // hidden dependency
        Logger.getInstance().log("paying " + o.id());
    }
}

// AFTER: dependencies explicit, one instance still (created at app start)
class PaymentService {
    private final Config config; private final Logger log;
    PaymentService(Config config, Logger log) { this.config = config; this.log = log; }
    void pay(Order o) { String key = config.get("stripe.key"); log.log("paying " + o.id()); }
}
// test: new PaymentService(fakeConfig, fakeLogger)

The fix keeps "one instance" as a lifetime decision made by the container (Spring @Singleton, Hilt @Singleton), not by the class.

When NOT to use it. Anything holding mutable business state, anything you want to fake in tests, anything per-user or per-request. OK uses: immutable config, stateless utilities, a thread-safe registry that is also injected.

Industry examples. Google's testing guidance calls static singletons a smell; Android's Dagger/Hilt @Singleton scope exists to give one instance without the static access.

Common interview traps.

  • Defending Singleton as "always fine". Say "one instance is fine, a global accessor is the problem".
  • Offering Singleton for a User or Cart; those are per-user.

notes.title: Factory Method: the idea
notes.html:
Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses (or implementations) decide which class to instantiate. The caller depends on a product interface, not on the concrete class.

Problem it solves: code that does if (type == "sms") new Sms() else if (type == "email") new Email() in many places.

+----------------+          +-------------------+
| Notification   |<>--------| NotifierFactory   |
| (interface)    |          +-------------------+
| + send(msg)    |          | + create(): Notif |
+----------------+          +-------------------+
   ^         ^                   ^           ^
   |         |                   |           |
 Sms       Email            SmsFactory   EmailFactory

Worked example. A notification module supports 3 channels today and 7 next year. With a factory method, adding a channel = 1 new class + 1 new factory; existing code untouched (Open/Closed principle).

Industry examples. java.util.Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getInstance(), Collection.iterator() (each collection returns its own iterator type), Android Fragment/ViewModelProvider.Factory, JDBC DriverManager.getConnection.

Everyday analogy. A franchise: head office says "serve a burger"; each city's branch decides which local burger.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "static factory method" (List.of) with the GoF Factory Method (subclass decides). Both are valid; know the difference.
  • Making the factory itself a god class with a giant switch.

notes.title: Factory Method in code: before and after
notes.html:
// BEFORE: caller knows every concrete class
class AlertService {
    void alert(String type, String msg) {
        if (type.equals("sms")) new SmsNotifier().send(msg);
        else if (type.equals("email")) new EmailNotifier().send(msg);
        // adding push = edit here AND in 5 other places
    }
}

// AFTER
interface Notifier { void send(String msg); }
class SmsNotifier implements Notifier { public void send(String m) { /* ... */ } }
class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { public void send(String m) { /* ... */ } }

abstract class AlertService {
    protected abstract Notifier createNotifier();        // the factory method
    void alert(String msg) { createNotifier().send(msg); }
}
class SmsAlertService extends AlertService {
    protected Notifier createNotifier() { return new SmsNotifier(); }
}

Simple variant (most interviews): a registry keyed by type, which avoids one subclass per product.

class NotifierFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Supplier<Notifier>> REG = Map.of(
        "sms", SmsNotifier::new, "email", EmailNotifier::new);
    static Notifier create(String type) {
        Supplier<Notifier> s = REG.get(type);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown " + type);
        return s.get();
    }
}

Kotlin variant:

interface Notifier { fun send(msg: String) }
class SmsNotifier : Notifier { override fun send(msg: String) { /* ... */ } }
class EmailNotifier : Notifier { override fun send(msg: String) { /* ... */ } }

object NotifierFactory {
    private val reg: Map<String, () -> Notifier> = mapOf("sms" to ::SmsNotifier, "email" to ::EmailNotifier)
    fun create(type: String): Notifier = reg[type]?.invoke() ?: error("unknown $type")
}

Decision gravity. Chosen to isolate "which class" in one spot. Alternatives: a plain switch (fine for 2 stable types), DI-provided maps. Breaks if products need different constructor arguments (leads to Abstract Factory or Builder). Reversible: callers only see the interface.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning null for unknown types instead of failing fast.
  • A registry plus a switch both present: pick one.

notes.title: When NOT to use Factory Method
notes.html:
Do not add a factory when there is one implementation and no variation expected. new ArrayList<>() needs no factory. A factory with one product is ceremony.

Signs you are over-doing it:

  • UserFactory that only calls new User(name).
  • A factory per class "for flexibility" nobody asked for (YAGNI).
  • Interface with a single implementation and a factory, in a 500-line module.

Use it when: (a) the concrete type depends on runtime input (config, payload type), (b) you must hide construction details (pooled or cached instances), (c) tests need to inject fakes, (d) a framework defines the skeleton and users supply the product.

Industry examples. Spring prefers DI over hand factories; Android Hilt generates factories for you. Google's Guava docs recommend static factories (ImmutableList.of) for naming and caching, not for polymorphism.

Everyday analogy. You do not hire a travel agent to cross the street.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "always use a factory". It is a smell if nothing varies.
  • Forgetting a simple alternative: a Map<String, Supplier<T>> or an enum with an abstract method.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Creational patterns centralize "how and which object"; use them only where something really varies.
  • Singleton: one instance. Variants: eager (simple, safe), synchronized (safe, slow), double-checked (needs volatile), holder idiom (lazy, lock-free), enum (also safe against reflection and serialization). Kotlin: object.
  • Singleton is often an anti-pattern: hidden global state, hard to test, tight coupling. Prefer DI with a container-managed single instance.
  • Factory Method: callers depend on a product interface; subclasses or a registry pick the concrete class. Adding a type = adding a class, not editing callers.
  • Do not build factories for a single implementation; fail fast on unknown types.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Singleton pattern, when would you use it, and what are the minimum ingredients to implement it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most-asked pattern; they check whether you understand controlled creation and its risk, not only the code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Singleton guarantees one instance of a class and gives a global access point. Ingredients: a private constructor so nobody else can new it, and a static method returning the single instance. Good for immutable config, a metrics registry or a connection-pool manager. It is global state with controlled creation, which is also why it is risky.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A 200 KB config parsed in 15 ms, hit by 1,000 requests per second, would cost 15 s of CPU per second if each request parsed it; parse once and share. JDK: Runtime.getRuntime(); Kotlin object; Spring "singleton" beans are container-managed, not static-field singletons.

+---------------------------+
| Config                    |
| - static instance: Config |
| - Config()                |
| + static getInstance()    |
+---------------------------+

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class Config {
    private static final Config INSTANCE = new Config();
    private Config() {}
    public static Config getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}
object Config { fun get(key: String): String = "..." }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling it just a global variable (it is global state with controlled creation).
  • Forgetting the private constructor.
  • Using it for per-user things like User or Cart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a Singleton risky? -> Hidden dependencies, shared mutable state, hard to test.
  2. Kotlin equivalent? -> object, compiler generates the static field and class-init.
  3. Spring singleton the same? -> No: one per container, not enforced by the class.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes the code. Senior says "one instance is fine, a global accessor is the problem" and prefers container-managed lifetime.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mutable static Cache singleton leaked data between tenants in tests and later in production.

questions.promptHtml: Why does double-checked locking need volatile? Walk through what can go wrong without it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the classic memory-model question; it separates memorised code from understanding reordering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: new Config() is three steps: allocate, run the constructor, assign the reference. Without volatile, the JIT or CPU can reorder so the reference is published before the constructor finishes, and another thread sees a non-null but half-built object. Since Java 5 (JSR-133), volatile forbids that reordering and guarantees visibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The first null check runs without a lock, so a reader can see the reference set early. With volatile, the write of the reference happens-after the constructor's writes, and the read sees them.

Thread A: allocate -> assign ref -> run ctor   (reordered)
Thread B:           sees ref != null, uses object -> reads default fields

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class Config {
    private static volatile Config instance;
    private Config() {}
    public static Config getInstance() {
        Config local = instance;
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (Config.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) instance = local = new Config();
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}
class Config private constructor() {
    companion object {
        @Volatile private var inst: Config? = null
        fun get(): Config = inst ?: synchronized(this) { inst ?: Config().also { inst = it } }
    }
}

The local variable avoids a second volatile read on the fast path.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Omitting volatile.
  • Explaining it without being able to say what reordering is.
  • Using it when the holder idiom would do.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it easy to get wrong? -> Yes; the holder idiom is simpler and lazy.
  2. What did Java 5 change? -> The memory model (JSR-133) gave volatile the needed happens-before semantics.
  3. Does it work for non-reference fields? -> Final fields of immutable objects have their own safe-publication rule; verify before relying.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "volatile for visibility". Senior explains the three steps and reordering, and recommends the holder idiom instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A DCL without volatile passed all tests and produced rare NPEs only on a many-core production host.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Factory Method pattern, and how is it different from a static factory method like List.of?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The terms are often confused; they also check whether you can say what problem it solves.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses or implementations decide which class to instantiate, so the caller depends on a product interface, not a concrete class. It solves if (type == "sms") new Sms() ... repeated in many places. A static factory method like List.of is just a named constructor; the GoF Factory Method has the subclass decide.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Notification (interface)        NotifierFactory { create(): Notification }
   ^          ^                    ^               ^
  Sms       Email             SmsFactory      EmailFactory

Adding a channel is one new class and one new factory, with no edits to callers: Open/Closed in practice. JDK examples: Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getInstance(), Collection.iterator() (each collection returns its own iterator), JDBC DriverManager.getConnection.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
abstract class AlertService {
    protected abstract Notifier createNotifier();   // the factory method
    void alert(String msg) { createNotifier().send(msg); }
}
class SmsAlertService extends AlertService {
    protected Notifier createNotifier() { return new SmsNotifier(); }
}
abstract class AlertService {
    protected abstract fun createNotifier(): Notifier
    fun alert(msg: String) = createNotifier().send(msg)
}
class SmsAlertService : AlertService() { override fun createNotifier() = SmsNotifier() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing static factory methods with the GoF pattern.
  • A factory that is a god class with a giant switch.
  • Returning null for unknown types.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Simplest version used in interviews? -> A registry Map<String, Supplier<Notifier>>.
  2. How does it relate to Open/Closed? -> New product, new class, no edits to callers.
  3. Factory Method vs Abstract Factory? -> One product vs a family of related products.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes a switch factory. Senior distinguishes variants, picks a registry or DI map, and fails fast on unknown types.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Adding WhatsApp to a system with 40 new SmsSender() call sites took 40 edits until a factory centralised creation.

questions.promptHtml: Why do many engineers call Singleton an anti-pattern, and what do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A mature answer defends neither extreme: keep single instance, drop global access.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Singleton is hidden global state: hidden dependencies (the constructor does not say it needs Config), hard to test (state leaks between tests, you cannot swap a fake), tight coupling to a concrete class, concurrency issues with mutable state, and it mixes the class's job with controlling its own lifetime. Instead I inject the dependency and let a container or the composition root create one instance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
// BEFORE: hidden, untestable
class PaymentService { void pay(Order o) { String key = Config.getInstance().get("stripe.key"); } }
// AFTER: explicit, one instance still created at app start
class PaymentService {
    private final Config config;
    PaymentService(Config config) { this.config = config; }
}

Lifetime becomes a wiring decision (Spring or Hilt @Singleton). OK uses: immutable config, stateless utilities, a thread-safe registry that is also injected. Never for per-user or per-request state.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Always fine" or "never use".
  • Singleton for User or Cart.
  • Forgetting tests share the instance, so order matters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Hilt @Singleton the same? -> One instance per component, but consumers receive it by injection.
  2. How do you test code using one? -> Introduce an interface and constructor parameter first.
  3. Mutable singleton in a multi-threaded service? -> Needs synchronization everywhere; avoid it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says Singleton is evil or defends it. Senior separates single instance from global access.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Tests passed alone and failed in suite order because a static Config kept a flag set by an earlier test.

questions.contextHtml:
A service opens a rate-limiter in getInstance(). Under load tests with 64 threads, the limiter allows about 2x the configured 100 req/s, and a debug log shows "RateLimiter created" twice at startup.

public static RateLimiter getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {
        instance = new RateLimiter(100);
    }
    return instance;
}

A teammate says the window is tiny and proposes synchronized on the whole method. Another says "just make it volatile".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug, evaluate both proposals and choose the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "volatile fixes it" or "the race window is too small to matter".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the instance needed at startup always? Is construction expensive or can it throw? Is getInstance on a hot path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Initialize it at startup in a single thread to stop the double creation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two threads pass the null check and each creates an instance, so each limiter allows 100 req/s; volatile alone does not make check-then-act atomic.
  4. How I'd verify: Log identity hash on creation; a 64-thread test with a CountDownLatch reproducing it.
  5. Root cause: Check-then-act race on an unsynchronized lazy field.
  6. Fix: Simplest: eager static final. If lazy is needed, the holder idiom: lazy, lock-free, JVM-guaranteed.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class RateLimiter {
    private RateLimiter() {}
    private static class Holder { static final RateLimiter I = new RateLimiter(); }
    public static RateLimiter getInstance() { return Holder.I; }
}
object RateLimiter { /* created on first access, thread-safe */ }

Method-level synchronized is correct but takes the lock on every call: with 16 threads x 1M calls, contention (1,000+ ns vs about 20 ns uncontended) adds up. 7. Prevention: Concurrency test with many threads asserting one identity; code review flag on if (instance == null). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not DCL here: correct only with volatile and easy to get wrong.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just volatile? -> It fixes visibility, not atomicity of check-then-act.
  • Is the race "rare"? -> It appears under load and at startup bursts, exactly when it hurts.
  • Rate limiter per tenant? -> Then it is not a Singleton; a map keyed by tenant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "tiny race window" produced two connection pools at deploy time and double the DB connections for a minute, tripping the DB's connection limit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "volatile" or "ignore".
  • Hire: identifies check-then-act and uses holder or eager.
  • Strong hire: compares costs of options and writes the concurrency test.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service migrates from 4-core to 64-core hosts. After the move, about 1 in 20,000 requests throws NullPointerException in PriceTable.lookup, and never on the old hosts or in staging. Stack excerpt and code:

java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot read field "rates" because "this.table" is null
  at com.shop.PriceTable.lookup(PriceTable.java:41)
  at com.shop.Pricing.price(Pricing.java:88)
public final class PriceTable {
    private static PriceTable instance;          // no volatile
    private final Map<String, Double> rates;
    private PriceTable() { rates = loadRates(); }   // 15 ms
    public static PriceTable getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (PriceTable.class) {
                if (instance == null) instance = new PriceTable();
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the new hardware or adds a null check around lookup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the NPE appear only soon after startup? JVM version and flags? Does the problem scale with core count?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Force initialization at startup (PriceTable.getInstance() in main) so no request races it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unsafe publication from DCL without volatile; a stale cache entry; a class-loading issue.
  4. How I'd verify: NPEs cluster in the first seconds after start; a jcstress-style test or a stress loop with many threads on a many-core box; read the code for volatile.
  5. Root cause: The reference can be visible before the constructor's writes (reordering); a thread sees a non-null instance with rates still null. More cores and the JIT make this likelier.
  6. Fix: Use the holder idiom (lazy, lock-free) or add volatile.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class PriceTable {
    private final Map<String, Double> rates;
    private PriceTable() { rates = loadRates(); }
    private static class Holder { static final PriceTable I = new PriceTable(); }
    public static PriceTable getInstance() { return Holder.I; }
}
object PriceTable { val rates: Map<String, Double> = loadRates() }
  1. Prevention: Static analysis rule for DCL without volatile; run concurrency tests on many cores; review checklist for lazy init.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No try/catch NullPointerException or retries; it hides the bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not reproducible in staging? -> Fewer cores and timing; the reorder window is rare.
  • Is final rates safe by itself? -> Final-field semantics help only when the reference does not escape in the constructor; do not rely on it here, use the holder.
  • Constructor throws? -> With the holder the class init fails with ExceptionInInitializerError and later NoClassDefFoundError.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A DCL bug passed two years on small hosts, then produced intermittent NPEs after a hardware upgrade; the fix was a three-line holder class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: null-check workaround.
  • Hire: identifies missing volatile and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: explains reordering, prefers holder idiom, adds eager-init mitigation and concurrency test.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments module uses Config.getInstance() and Logger.getInstance() inside PaymentService.pay. The test suite has 60 tests; run alone, each passes, run together, 3 fail depending on order (a test sets Config.set("retries","0") and never resets it). A new test needs a fake stripe key and cannot supply one.

class PaymentService {
    void pay(Order o) {
        String key = Config.getInstance().get("stripe.key");
        Logger.getInstance().log("paying " + o.id());
        // ...
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it for testability without losing the "one instance" property in production.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reset the singleton in @After" or reflection hacks to replace the instance.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Config mutable? Who else calls the singletons? Is there a DI container already?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reset state in a test base class to stop the flaky failures while refactoring.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Shared mutable static state causes order dependence; hidden dependencies prevent fakes.
  4. How I'd verify: Run tests in random order; the failing set changes.
  5. Root cause: Global access plus mutable state.
  6. Fix: Constructor injection; production wiring creates one instance in the composition root (or @Singleton in Spring/Hilt).

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class PaymentService {
    private final Config config; private final Logger log;
    PaymentService(Config config, Logger log) { this.config = config; this.log = log; }
    void pay(Order o) { String key = config.get("stripe.key"); log.log("paying " + o.id()); }
}
// test: new PaymentService(fakeConfig, fakeLogger)
class PaymentService(private val config: Config, private val log: Logger) {
    fun pay(o: Order) { val key = config.get("stripe.key"); log.log("paying ${o.id}") }
}
  1. Prevention: Lint or review rule against getInstance() inside business classes; random test order in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More constructor parameters; accept it. Not static mocking tools.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 400 call sites -> migrate incrementally: keep the static accessor delegating to the container, convert classes hot-first.
  • Is Config singleton ok if immutable? -> Yes; the problem is the global accessor and mutation.
  • Logger everywhere? -> Logging is often an accepted exception; hide behind an interface at boundaries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Random-order test runs exposed 14 hidden dependencies on one static config; moving them to constructors made tests parallel-safe.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: resets static in tests.
  • Hire: constructor injection with fakes.
  • Strong hire: keeps one instance via container, migration plan and random-order CI.

questions.contextHtml:
AlertService.alert(type, msg) has an if/else on "sms" and "email", and the same if appears in 5 other classes (AuditNotifier, RetryJob, ...). Product asks for push notifications this sprint and WhatsApp next quarter. Last time a channel was added, one of the 6 places was missed and critical alerts silently went nowhere for 3 days.

if (type.equals("sms")) new SmsNotifier().send(msg);
else if (type.equals("email")) new EmailNotifier().send(msg);
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change for push today, and how do you restructure so WhatsApp is a one-class change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds else if ("push") in all 6 places.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do notifiers need different constructor args (API keys)? Is the type string from config or user data? What happens on an unknown type?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add push in the one place the alert path uses, then centralize.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Duplicate type switch (shotgun surgery); no single owner of "which class".
  4. How I'd verify: grep '"sms"' to find all six places.
  5. Root cause: Callers know every concrete class.
  6. Fix: Notifier interface plus one factory (registry); callers ask the factory. Push becomes one class and one registry line; unknown type fails fast.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class NotifierFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Supplier<Notifier>> REG = Map.of(
        "sms", SmsNotifier::new, "email", EmailNotifier::new, "push", PushNotifier::new);
    static Notifier create(String type) {
        Supplier<Notifier> s = REG.get(type);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown " + type);
        return s.get();
    }
}
object NotifierFactory {
    private val reg: Map<String, () -> Notifier> =
        mapOf("sms" to ::SmsNotifier, "email" to ::EmailNotifier, "push" to ::PushNotifier)
    fun create(type: String): Notifier = reg[type]?.invoke() ?: error("unknown $type")
}
  1. Prevention: A test that every registered type produces a Notifier; ban new XNotifier() outside the factory.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No subclass-per-product Factory Method for this; a registry is enough. Never return null for unknown.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Notifiers need API keys -> inject config into the suppliers, or use DI-provided map.
  • Same channel needs several instances -> the factory returns new or cached by policy.
  • Different constructor args per type -> consider Abstract Factory or Builder.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A missed branch in one of six duplicated if ladders dropped critical alerts for 3 days; a single registry made the omission impossible.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits six places.
  • Hire: interface plus factory, fail-fast.
  • Strong hire: registry vs subclass choice, DI keys, test per registered type.

questions.contextHtml: A PR in a 500-line module adds UserFactory, IUserFactory, UserFactoryImpl and UserCreator, all just to call new User(name, email). The author says "for flexibility, and it is a pattern". There is one User class, no variation, no tests that need a fake. Another PR for ArrayList creation adds ListFactory.
questions.promptHtml: How do you review it, and when would you accept a factory?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Patterns are good practice, approve."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What varies here? Is there a second implementation planned? Does construction hide pooling or caching?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Request changes with specific reasons; no block on style.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: YAGNI violation, ceremony with one product, an interface with a single implementation in a small module.
  4. How I'd verify: Search for any other User implementation or any test needing a fake; none.
  5. Root cause: A pattern applied because it is a pattern, not because something varies.
  6. Fix: Delete the factory layers; keep new User(name, email). Accept a factory when: (a) the concrete type depends on runtime input, (b) construction must be hidden (pooled or cached instances), (c) tests must inject fakes, (d) a framework defines the skeleton and users supply the product.
  7. Prevention: Rule of three: add the abstraction at the second or third real variant.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Adding a factory later is cheap and reversible, so waiting costs little. Also point out a simpler alternative if variation arrives: Map<String, Supplier<T>> or an enum with an abstract method.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Static factory User.of(name) for naming? -> Fine; Guava recommends it for naming and caching, not for polymorphism.
  • Hilt or Spring already creates it -> then the framework is the factory.
  • Author says "we may add AdminUser later" -> add the factory then.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A module with a factory per class had 3x the files and onboarding took a week; deleting single-product factories made the dependency graph readable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves for "good practice".
  • Hire: invokes YAGNI and names when a factory fits.
  • Strong hire: lists criteria, cheap alternatives, and reversibility.

questions.contextHtml: A codebase has 40 call sites doing new SmsSender("key"). Product wants WhatsApp, and ops wants to switch SMS vendors per country (India vs EU), with a kill switch. A teammate proposes Abstract Factory plus Builder plus Prototype "to be ready for anything". You have two days.
questions.promptHtml: Which creational approach do you pick and what do you leave out?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Recites all 23 patterns or applies several at once.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What varies: vendor, channel, or both? Is the choice by config or runtime data (country)? Do senders need different constructor args?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Introduce one Sender interface and one factory; leave call sites untouched until moved.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The real variation is "which sender for this country and channel", which is one factory with a registry; families of objects (Abstract Factory) are not required yet.
  4. How I'd verify: List how many distinct senders and which constructor args differ.
  5. Root cause: new glues 40 call sites to one concrete class.
  6. Fix: Sender interface, SenderFactory.create(channel, country) backed by a registry or DI map; migrate call sites in batches (grep for new SmsSender); kill switch is a config flag consulted by the factory.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Sender { void send(String to, String msg); }
class SenderFactory {
    private final Map<String, Supplier<Sender>> reg;
    SenderFactory(Map<String, Supplier<Sender>> reg) { this.reg = reg; }
    Sender create(String channel, String country) {
        Supplier<Sender> s = reg.get(channel + ":" + country);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no sender " + channel + ":" + country);
        return s.get();
    }
}
class SenderFactory(private val reg: Map<String, () -> Sender>) {
    fun create(channel: String, country: String): Sender =
        reg["$channel:$country"]?.invoke() ?: error("no sender $channel:$country")
}
  1. Prevention: Lint ban on new SmsSender; contract test per sender.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No Prototype (no copying need), no Builder until constructors get 5+ optional args; Abstract Factory only if channel and vendor must be swapped as a family.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Senders need a pooled HTTP client -> factory gives them a shared instance by injection.
  • Pick the vendor at runtime by load? -> A routing decorator over the senders, outside the factory.
  • 40 sites migration risk -> mechanical rename, one PR per module.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added three patterns for "future flexibility"; a single factory with a map later covered every real change in two years.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names patterns without need.
  • Hire: single factory, interface, incremental migration.
  • Strong hire: states what is not built and when it would become necessary.

questions.contextHtml:
A licence-manager Singleton (private constructor, holder idiom) allows 10 seats. QA reports 12 concurrent users got in. Findings: (1) a plugin deserializes a saved session object that contains the manager, (2) the app runs on an app server where two web apps each ship the jar in their own class loader, (3) a test helper calls the constructor via reflection.

public final class LicenseManager implements Serializable {
    private LicenseManager() {}
    private static class Holder { static final LicenseManager I = new LicenseManager(); }
    public static LicenseManager getInstance() { return Holder.I; }
    private final AtomicInteger seats = new AtomicInteger(10);
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain each way the guarantee breaks and how you fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A private constructor guarantees one instance."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the limit hold across processes (then a Singleton cannot do it)? Does anything need serialization? Which app server and class-loader layout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the plugin's deserialization path and enforce the limit server-side while redesigning.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Deserialization creates a new object; separate class loaders give one "singleton" per loader; reflection with setAccessible(true) bypasses the private constructor.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare identityHashCode and getClass().getClassLoader() of instances; unit test with ObjectOutputStream round trip.
  5. Root cause: A Singleton is one per class loader and only as strong as its construction path.
  6. Fix: For serialization add readResolve() returning the instance, or use an enum, which the JVM protects against reflection and serialization. For class loaders, move the jar to a shared parent loader. For cross-process limits, use a shared store (DB row or Redis counter), not an in-memory Singleton.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public enum LicenseManager {
    INSTANCE;
    private final AtomicInteger seats = new AtomicInteger(10);
    public boolean acquire() { return seats.getAndUpdate(n -> n > 0 ? n - 1 : n) > 0; }
}
object LicenseManager {
    private val seats = AtomicInteger(10)
    fun acquire(): Boolean = seats.getAndUpdate { if (it > 0) it - 1 else it } > 0
}
  1. Prevention: Tests for serialization and multi-loader; rule that process-wide limits live in shared storage.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: An enum cannot extend a class and is eager; acceptable here. Kotlin object is still per class loader and breakable via reflection (verify for your platform).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multiple JVMs behind a load balancer -> in-memory singleton cannot enforce a global limit; use a database or distributed counter.
  • Reflection defence in constructor? -> Throw if INSTANCE exists; the enum makes it unnecessary.
  • Why not just synchronized? -> Unrelated to creation paths; the bug is extra instances.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "singleton" connection limiter existed once per web app on a shared server and doubled the limit until someone printed class-loader names.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts the private constructor.
  • Hire: names reflection, serialization, class loaders with fixes.
  • Strong hire: also says an in-memory singleton cannot enforce a cross-process limit.

questions.contextHtml:
After a deploy, a service starts but every request to /prices returns 500. Logs:

java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
  at com.shop.PriceApi.handle(PriceApi.java:22)
Caused by: java.io.FileNotFoundException: /etc/shop/rates.json
  at com.shop.RateConfig.<clinit>(RateConfig.java:9)
...
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.shop.RateConfig
  at com.shop.PriceApi.handle(PriceApi.java:22)     (all later requests)
public final class RateConfig {
    private static final RateConfig INSTANCE = new RateConfig();   // reads /etc/shop/rates.json
    private RateConfig() { /* load file */ }
    public static RateConfig getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}

The file was present on the previous hosts; it appeared 40 s after the container started on the new platform. Other endpoints work fine.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why one missing file poisons the endpoint permanently, and how you fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the service" with no design change, or "eager singletons are not thread safe".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When is the class first touched (startup or first request)? Is the file mounted after start? Is a restart acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the instance once the file exists (the failed class state cannot recover in the same JVM).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Static initializer threw; the JVM marks the class unusable (NoClassDefFoundError afterwards); the file mount was late.
  4. How I'd verify: The first stack has ExceptionInInitializerError with the cause; later ones show "Could not initialize class".
  5. Root cause: Heavy, fallible work in a static initializer; eager init makes one failure permanent for the process.
  6. Fix: Load config at startup in the composition root with retries and a clear fail-fast, inject it; or hold the loading in an explicit init().

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class RateConfig {
    private final Map<String, Double> rates;
    public RateConfig(Path file) { this.rates = load(file); }   // plain constructor, can throw normally
}
// main: wait for file (bounded), new RateConfig(path), pass to services
class RateConfig(file: Path) { val rates: Map<String, Double> = load(file) }
// main: retry with backoff, then wire services
  1. Prevention: Readiness probe waits for the config; start-up smoke test; no IO in static initializers.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a lazy holder with the same failing load (same permanence); not catching and ignoring the failure.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did only /prices fail? -> Only that path touched the class; eager means "at first use of the class", not necessarily at startup.
  • Hot-reload config? -> Use an injected holder object with an atomic reference, not a static initializer.
  • Can the class recover? -> No, not in the same class loader.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A static initializer reading a mounted secret failed once at boot and left one endpoint returning 500 for hours, until it was restarted and later moved to explicit start-up wiring.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts and moves on.
  • Hire: explains ExceptionInInitializerError then NoClassDefFoundError and moves loading out.
  • Strong hire: fail-fast startup, readiness probe, config reload design.
